strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with an intuitive framing (plasticity as an average rate of change) and informative figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3) that make the argument easy to follow.

The experimental effort is substantial: component-wise finetuning of ViT-Base on 11 benchmarks, 4 learning rates, 3 seeds (~800 runs), plus a larger ViT-Huge plasticity study, with detailed hyperparameters, architectures, and preprocessing in the appendix, giving good reproducibility.

The plasticity analysis is consistent: the empirical ranking (MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1) is stable across datasets and model sizes, and the paper checks the predicted sequence-length dependence on ViT-Huge, lending internal coherence.

Theoretical upper bounds are provided with full proofs (Propositions 1-4, Appendix B), and the authors are transparent that the bounds are loose (Fig. 6) and that the plasticity estimate is an average rather than a Lipschitz constant.
A plausible mechanism is offered and partially evidenced (gradient-norm and validation-loss curves track the plasticity ranking), and a limitations section is included.
weaknesses: The central causal claim ('high plasticity leads to better finetuning') is supported only by correlation. Plasticity is computed on the frozen, pretrained modules (Definition 1), but finetuning changes these weights, so the measure does not directly characterize the trainability of the modules it is used to explain.

A major confound undermines the headline comparison: the high-plasticity modules (MHA, FC1, FC2) each have 28M trainable parameters (33%), while LN1 and LN2 have only 18K (0.02%). The overall ~1% gap between these groups is plausibly explained by parameter count rather than plasticity. Within same-size groups the differences collapse to 0.1-0.5% (e.g., MHA vs FC1 = 0.07%, not significant per Table 1), which is at the noise level for 3 seeds.

The claimed ordering is not actually consistent: FC1 beats MHA on Cifar10 (99.09 vs 98.91), and FC2/FC1 beat MHA on Sketch (69.49/69.31 vs 69.23), contradicting the 'MHA highest plasticity -> best' narrative the paper leans on. The paper concedes 'except for FC1' but does not reconcile this with the theory.

Definition 1 uses 'the uniform distribution over the set of distinct pairs of sequences of tokens in (R^d)^n,' which is not a well-defined probability distribution on a continuous space; the experiments also compute rates of change from cross-domain pairs (ImageNet vs downstream), which does not match the stated distribution, so definition and implementation are inconsistent.

The theoretical 'ranking' is heuristic. The bounds are orders of magnitude apart (the attention bound is ~10^6, Fig. 6), so comparing loose upper bounds across different modules does not rigorously rank their actual plasticity. The ranking argument relies on comparing bound tightness (|gamma|_inf vs ||W||_2) rather than on the quantities of interest, and the tools used (Frobenius submultiplicativity, softmax Lipschitz) are standard; Proposition 3 largely restates Castin et al. (2024, Thm 3.3).

Novelty is limited. The practical guidance (finetuning attention or feedforward layers is effective) is already established (e.g., Touvron et al. 2022; Ye et al. 2023), and the plasticity measure is scale/norm dependent, so it may largely reflect weight norms (attention/FFN weights vs. normalizing LayerNorm weights) rather than a distinct functional property.

Large gradient norms are presented as the mechanism for better adaptation, but the work does not establish that larger gradients cause better generalization (its own setup clips gradients at norm 1), leaving the causal story incomplete.

strengths: Offers a fresh perspective that connects module smoothness to finetuning adaptability, explicitly inverting the conventional wisdom that smoothness is always desirable. This framing (plasticity as average rate of change) is conceptually interesting and could motivate future adaptation-method design.

Provides explicit theoretical upper bounds for each component type (LayerNorm, feedforward, multi-head attention) with full proofs in the appendix, plus a refinement (Proposition 4) that improves the sequence-length dependence to sqrt(n).

The empirical study is substantial in scope: two model scales (ViT-Base 86M, ViT-Huge 632M), 11 classification/domain-shift benchmarks, 4 learning rates, 3 seeds, and ~800 finetuning runs, with training-dynamics analysis (gradient norms, validation loss) to complement accuracy.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: architecture details, pretrained checkpoints, preprocessing, learning-rate grids, memory accounting, and a code snippet are provided.
The limitations section is honest and points to plausible extensions (tailored optimizers, LLM decoders, combining with LoRA).
weaknesses: The theoretical ranking is built on upper bounds that are admitted to be extremely loose (the attention bound is orders of magnitude larger, ~1e6, than the others). Comparing loose upper bounds does not rigorously establish a ranking of actual plasticity; the derivation that ||gamma||_inf is 'comparable to ||W||_inf which is smaller than the spectral norm' is a hand-wavy heuristic assuming entries are 'in a similar range', not a theorem.

Definition 1 defines plasticity as an expectation under the uniform distribution over all distinct pairs of sequences in (R^d)^n, which does not exist for unbounded R^d. In practice the quantity is computed from pairs of pretraining vs. downstream embeddings, so the theory and the experiment do not measure the same object. The claim that plasticity is 'an intrinsic property of the components and their weights' is therefore not supported, since the measured value clearly depends on the input pair distribution.

The central causal claim (high plasticity -> better finetuning) is only correlational and is confounded by trainable-parameter count: MHA/FC1/FC2 have 28M parameters versus 18K for LN1/LN2 (a ~1500x difference). The headline result (MHA/FC > LN) can be explained by capacity alone. The within-size comparisons that would control for this show only tiny gaps (e.g., MHA 90.8 vs FC1 90.7 vs FC2 90.3; LN1 89.8 vs LN2 89.9), and Table 1 reports average MHA-vs-FC1 decrease of 0.07% (not significant). No intervention that manipulates plasticity while holding capacity fixed is provided, so the mechanism is not established.

Effect sizes are small and practical significance is limited: full finetuning reaches 90.9 avg, essentially tied with finetuning MHA alone (90.8), and the best-to-worst spread across selective configurations is ~1% absolute. This weakens the 'key takeaway for practitioners'.

The practical recommendation (prioritize attention and feedforward layers) largely restates prior empirical findings (Touvron et al., 2022 on attention-only tuning; Ye et al., 2023 on feedforward), so the novel contribution reduces to the explanatory framing rather than a new actionable method.

The link between input-output smoothness and weight-output gradients (via Bethune et al.) is invoked informally to argue that high plasticity 'allows large gradient norms' and thus faster adaptation; this is a heuristic, not a demonstrated causal path, and the observed gradient-norm ordering is again a correlation among confounded configurations.

The theoretical ranking does not distinguish FC1 vs FC2 nor LN1 vs LN2; those orderings are asserted empirically and then presented as refining the theory, which is a post-hoc alignment rather than a prediction. The terminology 'plasticity' also conflicts with its established meaning in the continual-learning literature (e.g., Lyle et al., 2023; Dohare et al., 2024), risking confusion.
Illustrative claims (Fig. 1: smooth modules 'constrain gradient norms' leading to 'slow descent') are presented as explanation but are not rigorously tied to the measured quantities.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated perspective: reframing smoothness as a potential liability for finetuning, with a formal 'plasticity' measure (Definition 1) defined as an average rate of change, and an explicit departure from the conventional 'smoothness is good' wisdom.

Rigorous and self-contained theoretical analysis: Propositions 1-4 provide clean upper bounds on the plasticity of LayerNorm, feedforward layers, and multi-head self-attention, with complete proofs in the appendix, yielding a principled component ranking (MHA -> FC1/FC2 -> LN2/LN1).

Comprehensive, large-scale empirical study: 11 diverse classification benchmarks, two ViT scales (86M and 632M), ~800 finetuning runs with multiple seeds and a learning-rate sweep, plus cross-checks of the plasticity ranking across datasets and model sizes.

The empirical plasticity ranking consistently matches the theoretical predictions, and the mechanistic observation that higher plasticity correlates with larger gradient norms and steeper validation-loss descent is a genuinely interesting and coherent story.
Good reproducibility practices: detailed architecture tables, hyperparameters, data-split protocols, and memory-load accounting are all reported.
Honest and appropriate limitations discussion (vision-only scope, no tailored optimizer, extension to LLMs sketched but not tested).
weaknesses: The central practical claim ('consistently better finetuning performance') is overstated. The average accuracy spread is small (MHA 90.8 vs LN1 89.8), and the per-benchmark results are inconsistent: LayerNorms actually outperform MHA/FC on Gaussian Noise, Snow, Flowers102, and Pet. Only LN1/LN2 show statistically significant differences from MHA (Table 1), with MHA vs FC2 being just 0.44%.

Confound between parameter count and component type: MHA/FC1/FC2 have 28M trainable parameters while LN1/LN2 have only 18K. The headline ranking conflates plasticity with model capacity, and the within-size comparisons are not enough to fully rule this out as an explanation for the performance gap.

Definition 1 posits a 'uniform distribution over the set of distinct pairs of sequences of tokens in (R^d)^n', which is not well-defined on an unbounded continuous space; the quantity is only ever operationalized as an empirical average over data, so the measure lacks a rigorous probabilistic foundation.

The link from plasticity to finetuning benefit remains essentially correlational. The argument leans on Béthune et al. (2024) (Lipschitz regularization ~ bounding parameter gradients) rather than a direct derivation, and the theoretical bounds are extremely loose (the attention bound is orders of magnitude larger than the others), with the ranking argument resting on heuristic assumptions ('spectral norms above 1 in practice').

Limited novelty relative to prior empirical work: Touvron et al. (2022) already showed attention-only tuning is beneficial and Zhao et al. (2024) / Ye et al. (2023) studied LayerNorm/feedforward tuning, so the new element is mainly the plasticity framing rather than a new adaptation method or a large practical gain.

Minor issues: the background typo 'Lipschitz continuous if there exists a constant K ≤ 0' should be K ≥ 0; the appendix figure captions are highly repetitive; the improvement over linear probing is used as the headline metric but linear probing is a weak baseline that inflates relative gains.

strengths: Provides a clear, well-motivated new perspective: it formalizes 'plasticity' as the average rate of change (Def. 1), essentially the average Lipschitz ratio, and uses it to reason about which transformer components to prioritize during finetuning. This reframes smoothness as a limitation rather than a virtue for adaptation, which is a genuinely interesting angle.

The empirical study is unusually extensive and internally consistent: ~1,000 finetuning runs on 11 benchmarks, ViT-Base/Large/Huge, SGD and Adam, full-data and VTAB low-data regimes, and plasticity measurements extended to DINOv3 (7B) and GPT2. The plasticity ranking (MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1) is reproduced across benchmarks and architectures (Figs. 3, 4, 8-18), giving the empirical claims real weight.

Presentation and reproducibility are strong: figures are informative (Fig. 1 links plasticity to gradient norms and loss descent), the appendix gives full hyperparameters, memory tables, and preprocessing details, code is released, and the carbon footprint is reported. Limitations are stated honestly.

The within-size-group comparisons (MHA/FC1/FC2 at 28M params; LN1/LN2 at 18K params) partially control for the parameter-count confound and still respect the predicted plasticity ordering, which lends some credibility to the mechanism beyond raw capacity.

The theoretical propositions (adapting Castin et al.'s attention Lipschitz bound) are technically correct as upper bounds, and the numerical computation of bounds on ViT-Base (Fig. 7) is a reasonable sanity check that the ordering matches the measured plasticity.
weaknesses: The headline 'theoretical ranking' is not rigorous: it is obtained by comparing the magnitudes of loose upper bounds (Prop. 1-4). A larger upper bound does not imply a larger true plasticity, and the argument that 'spectral norms are above 1 in practice' is an empirical assumption, not a proof. The theory therefore provides intuition rather than a principled ranking, which is a weaker claim than the paper's framing suggests.

Effect sizes are modest and the statistical story is thin. The overall gap between the best (MHA, 90.75) and worst (LN1, 89.82) configuration is ~1%, and full finetuning (90.90) barely exceeds MHA. Significance is only tested against MHA, so many pairwise comparisons (e.g., FC2 vs LN1) are likely not significant, yet the paper repeatedly asserts a strong, consistent ordering.

The cross-group claim that 'high plasticity -> better finetuning' is confounded with trainable parameter count (28M for MHA/FC1/FC2 vs 18K for LN1/LN2). The paper's own defense ('parameter count alone does not determine performance') is anecdotal, and the within-size comparisons only partially address this; a controlled experiment matching capacity across component types is missing.

The mechanism connecting plasticity to finetuning performance is correlational. The link to parameter-gradient norms rests on a cited theorem (Bethune et al., 2024) plus intuition, and the paper itself concedes the relationship is not expected to be linear. The central causal claim (non-smoothness facilitates adaptation) is therefore not directly established.

Prop. 1 relies on the strong assumption that all tokens at a given position share the same mean and standard deviation, justified informally via ImageNet normalization and a shared embedding layer; the bound also depends on a minimum standard deviation sigma, so it is not clearly comparable in scale to the spectral-norm bounds used for the other modules.

The term 'plasticity' is borrowed but redefined relative to its established meaning in continual learning (e.g., Dohare et al., 2024), which risks confusion; the measure is simply an average Lipschitz ratio, and its added value over existing average-smoothness notions (Ashlagi et al., 2021) is not fully articulated.

Scope is limited to image-classification finetuning of ViTs; the extension to decoder-only LLMs is asserted (Section 4, DINOv3/GPT2 plasticity only) but not demonstrated for finetuning, so the practical guidance is narrower than the framing implies.
Minor issues: the Lipschitz definition states 'K <= 0' where K >= 0 is intended; some claims (e.g., LN finetuning outperforming LoRA) are supported only via a single cross-paper comparison.

strengths: Substantial, systematic empirical effort: ~1,000 finetuning runs over 11 benchmarks, three model scales, SGD and Adam, plus VTAB low-data and ViT-Large extensions, with good reproducibility reporting (code, hyperparameters, carbon footprint).

The plasticity measure, while simple, yields a consistent empirical ranking (MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1) that holds across supervised ViTs, DINOv3, and GPT-2, which is a genuinely useful descriptive observation.

The gradient-norm and validation-loss-descent analyses (Figs. 21-53) provide a plausible mechanistic link between component plasticity and optimization behavior, and the presentation is clear and well-organized with an extensive appendix.
Limitations and ethics are discussed honestly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The 'theoretical ranking' is not soundly established. The paper compares upper bounds on plasticity, but a looser/larger upper bound does not imply higher plasticity. The authors themselves concede (App. E.1.1) that the MHA bound is ~10^6 and that the scale gap is due to the difficulty of bounding attention's Lipschitz constant. Inferring a component ordering from the looseness of bounds is not valid inference; the ranking is effectively empirical and the theory is largely decorative.

The central empirical claim is overstated. The abstract/intro promise that high plasticity 'consistently leads to better finetuning performance,' yet the average gaps are ~1% and the ordering is frequently reversed: LN2/LN1 win on Gaussian Noise, Flowers102, and Pet (Table 8). Full finetuning (90.90) beats every single-component configuration (best 90.75), so the practical payoff is marginal.

Parameter-count confound. The high-plasticity configurations (MHA/FC1/FC2) have ~28M trainable parameters versus ~18K for the LayerNorms. Larger gradient norms and better accuracy could partly reflect parameter count rather than plasticity; the paper does not cleanly control for this.

Definition 1 is mathematically ill-posed: there is no uniform distribution over the space of token sequences, and the operationalized plasticity is data-dependent (computed using downstream images). This contradicts the claim in Section 5.1 that plasticity is 'an intrinsic property of the components and their weights.'

Limited novelty relative to the framing. The actionable takeaway (prioritize attention, then FFN) essentially re-derives the known result of Touvron et al. (2022), and the plasticity/large-gradient intuition echoes existing plasticity literature (e.g., Lyle et al., 2023; Dohare et al., 2024). The 'departure from the prevailing smoothness assumption' is asserted more than demonstrated.

Practical relevance is constrained by the isolated single-component protocol (necessary for the analysis but not how PEFT is used in practice), and the theory's connection to finetuning rests on a loose conceptual appeal to Bethune et al. (2024) rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

strengths: Novel and useful framing: the paper reframes transformer component selection for finetuning through the lens of 'plasticity' (average rate of change), providing a principled, quantitative alternative to the prevailing 'smoothness is good' narrative and connecting it to input-vs-weight smoothness via Béthune et al. (2024).

Large-scale, well-controlled empirical study: ~1000 finetuning runs across 11 benchmarks, three ViT sizes (86M/307M/632M), SGD and Adam, multiple seeds and learning-rate sweeps, plus a VTAB low-data regime, isolating one component type at a time to avoid combinatorial confounders.

Theoretical analysis per component: Propositions 1-4 derive upper bounds on plasticity for LayerNorm, feedforward linear layers, and (single/multi-head) self-attention, with a tighter sequence-length-dependent bound (Prop. 4), and the numerically computed bounds are shown to match the empirical ranking.

Credible controls for the parameter-count confounder: within-group comparisons (MHA/FC1/FC2 at 28M parameters, and LN1/LN2 at 18K parameters) both respect the predicted plasticity ordering, so the effect is not purely an artifact of trainable-parameter count; the relative-gain-over-linear-probing metric further normalizes comparisons.

Generalization beyond the main setting: the plasticity ranking is reproduced on DINOv3 (7B, self-supervised) and GPT2 (decoder-only), supporting the claim that plasticity is an intrinsic property of modules and weights rather than a ViT-specific artifact.

Good reproducibility and research ethics: open-source code, detailed hyperparameters and preprocessing, deterministic splits, and an explicit carbon-footprint estimate; limitations and the correlational nature of some claims are acknowledged.

Practically relevant and stable finding: high-plasticity components (MHA, FC1) yield better and more stable finetuning across learning rates and seeds, with gradient-norm and validation-loss trajectories consistent with the proposed mechanism (Figs. 5, 21-53).
weaknesses: The theoretical 'ranking' is heuristic rather than a rigorous theorem. The bounds have different functional forms and the attention bound is several orders of magnitude looser (O(10^6)), so the cross-module ordering rests on informal arguments about spectral norms exceeding 1 and typical value ranges; comparing bounds of different scales is not formally well-defined, and the paper itself notes the gap between the Lipschitz bound and the average rate of change can be considerable.

The central causal claim (high plasticity → better finetuning) is established by correlation, not intervention. The proposed mechanism (larger gradient norms) is asserted and only indirectly supported by gradient-norm plots; no experiment directly perturbs plasticity (e.g., Lipschitz regularization of a plastic module) to show downstream performance degrades, which would substantially strengthen the causal story.

Effect sizes are modest and the 'consistency' claim is overstated. The average gap between best (MHA, 90.8) and worst (LN1, 89.8) is ~1%, and the ranking is violated or ambiguous on several benchmarks (Gaussian Noise, Snow, Pets, Flowers102 favor LayerNorms), where the paper leans on aggregate averages. The 28M-vs-18K parameter gap between module groups remains a residual confounder despite the relative-gain metric.

Terminology collision: 'plasticity' here denotes input-sensitivity (low smoothness), whereas a substantial literature (e.g., Lyle et al. 2023; Dohare et al. 2024 — the latter cited) uses 'plasticity' to mean the ability to learn/adapt weights, including the well-known 'loss of plasticity' phenomenon. This conceptual overlap is not disambiguated and risks confusing readers.

Mismatch between the formal definition and its estimator: Definition 1 is an expectation over the uniform distribution on all distinct token-sequence pairs in R^{d×n}, but empirically the measure is computed on embedded real images. The relationship between the idealized measure and the data-based estimate is not reconciled, and the 'two regimes' threshold at 1 is tied to the unnormalized definition.

Limited incremental novelty for practitioners: the headline recommendation (prioritize attention and first feedforward layer) partially overlaps with existing empirical findings (e.g., Touvron et al. 2022 on attention tuning), and the paper does not benchmark against strong PEFT baselines in the main experiments (only a passing LoRA comparison), leaving unclear how much the plasticity guidance adds over established heuristics.
